transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Well, the country is coming off a night of huge swings toward Democratic candidates in
key midterm election races, especially in the southern U.S.
NPR's Stephen Fowler reports much of that is from increased black voter turnout.
North and South Carolina flipped U.S. Senate seats. Georgia elected a Democratic governor,
the first black woman to hold that office in U.S. history, and in Alabama, Congressman
Shamari figures held on in a district gerrymandered to limit black voting power.
The Senate race in Mississippi, a state that voted for Trump by 24 points and has the highest
share of black voters in the country, is too close to call.
It's not just federal races. Democrats took control of several state legislative chambers
and flipped seats across the region. Stephen Fowler, NPR News.
It was a difficult night for President Trump, who blamed Republican candidates and lashed
out at media. But NPR's Franco Ordonez reports that Trump made this election a referendum
on his presidency.
Trump made himself the central figure in this midterm election, crisscrossing the country,
hoping to turn out supporters and offset nationwide concerns about the high cost of living.
Republicans are now at a crossroads faced with questions about if and how to separate
themselves from the person who has defined the party over the last decade. On the one
hand, they don't want to repeat the mistakes of this midterm. On the other, Republicans
don't want to abandon Trump and risk alienating his supporters who have become the core of
the party. Franco Ordonez, NPR News.
Vice President J.D. Vance says in an online post today, quote, "Our voters showed up,"
but he says many of them voted for Democrats in part because of inflation and the U.S.
war in Iran. In Florida, outgoing Governor Ron DeSantis says the GOP will be reassessing
the Democratic blowout in races across the United States.
Let's just be clear about what happened last night. This is close to an extinction level
event for Republicans in many parts of the country, as we have seen probably in the last
hundred years. But Florida Republicans are celebrating still one major win, the election
of Byron Donald's for governor. Speaker of the House Mike Johnson will not stay on as
minority leader when Democrats assume the House majority in January, according to a
source familiar with Johnson's plans, who has not authorized to discuss them publicly.
House Republicans will choose a replacement for Johnson when they hold leadership elections
for the new Congress on November 10th. Looking at reaction from overseas, the top Iranian
negotiator says the results of the midterms show Americans rejecting a possible return
to war. The Iranian speaker of parliament, Mohammad Ghali, said that whether it was out
of conscience or the pressure of living expenses, Americans said no to the war.
We're listening to NPR News. Big tech company Google says it's making changes to its education
software. It says this will give schools more control over artificial intelligence tools.
And Paris Sequoia Corrillo reports there's one large caveat.
Google Classroom, the dominant software suite used by more than 100 million students, will
now give schools the option to turn off A.I. The features in question mostly revolve around
the company's flagship chatbot Gemini. But this announcement also says that if schools
decide they do not want A.I., Google search would be disabled entirely. The move comes
as school districts around the country are reevaluating the way technology operates in
classrooms. The two largest in the country, the Los Angeles Unified School District and
New York City Public Schools, recently announced limitations around A.I. and screen time for
students. Google says the changes will roll out in the coming months.
Sequoia Corrillo reporting. A NASA space telescope's re-entering Earth's atmosphere. Here's NPR's
Jeff Brumfield.
It was called SWIFT and it detected bursts of gamma rays from some of the most powerful
events in the universe. SWIFT saw black holes shred nearby stars and the massive explosions
from dead stars colliding together. When it spotted something day or night, it sent text
alerts to scientists like Kim Page at the University of Leicester.
It does kind of feel like losing one of the family. I mean, I've thought about SWIFT
every day for 22 years.
NASA has no immediate plans to replace SWIFT, but scientists will continue to study its
data well into the future. Jeff Brumfield, NPR News.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Democrats flip Senate seats in North and South Carolina and win Georgia governor race in midterms
Trump blames Republican candidates and media after midterm losses, making election a referendum on his presidency
Vance says voters showed up but many backed Democrats over inflation and the Iran war
DeSantis calls Democratic midterm wins near extinction event for Republicans; Byron Donalds wins Florida governor
Speaker Mike Johnson will not remain minority leader when Democrats take House majority in January
Iranian speaker says Americans rejected war with Iran through midterm votes
Google Classroom to let schools turn off AI features, though disabling them also disables Google search
NASA's SWIFT space telescope re-enters Earth's atmosphere after 22 years detecting gamma-ray bursts
